{{Short description|Extension of the classical tensor calculus}}
[[File:Dannebrog.jpg|thumb|200px|The surface of a flag in the wind is an example of a deforming manifold.]]

The '''calculus of moving surfaces''' ('''CMS''') <ref>Grinfeld, P. (2010). "Hamiltonian Dynamic Equations for Fluid Films". Studies in Applied Mathematics. {{doi|10.1111/j.1467-9590.2010.00485.x}}. {{ISSN|0022-2526}}.</ref> is an extension of the classical [[Tensor|tensor calculus]] to deforming [[manifold]]s. Central to the CMS is the tensorial time derivative <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> whose original definition <ref>J. Hadamard, Leçons Sur La Propagation Des Ondes Et Les Équations de l'Hydrodynamique. Paris: Hermann, 1903.</ref> was put forth by [[Jacques Hadamard]]. It plays the role analogous to that of the [[covariant derivative]] <math>\nabla _{\alpha }</math> on [[Differentiable manifold|differential manifolds]] in that it produces a [[tensor]] when applied to a tensor.


Suppose that <math>\Sigma_t</math> is the evolution of the [[surface (differential geometry)|surface]] <math>\Sigma</math> indexed by a time-like parameter <math>t</math>. The definitions of the surface [[velocity]] <math>C</math> and the [[operator (mathematics)|operator]] <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> are the [[geometric]] foundations of the CMS. The velocity C is the [[rate (mathematics)|rate]] of deformation of the surface <math>\Sigma</math> in the instantaneous [[Surface normal|normal]] direction. The value of <math>C</math> at a point <math>P</math> is defined as the [[limit of a function|limit]]

<math display="block">C=\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{\text{Distance}(P,P^*)}{h}</math>

where <math>P^{*}</math> is the point on <math>\Sigma_{t+h}</math> that lies on the straight line perpendicular to <math>\Sigma_{t}</math> at point P. This definition is illustrated in the first geometric figure below. The velocity <math>C</math> is a signed quantity: it is positive when <math>\overline{PP^{*}}</math> points in the direction of the chosen normal, and negative otherwise. The relationship between <math>\Sigma_{t}</math> and <math>C</math> is analogous to the relationship between location and velocity in elementary calculus:&nbsp;knowing either quantity allows one to construct the other by [[Derivative|differentiation]] or [[Initial value problem|integration]].

[[File:C3x3t.png|thumb|350px|Geometric construction of the surface velocity C]]
[[File:DFdt3x3t.png|thumb|350px|Geometric construction of the <math>\delta/\delta t</math>-derivative of an invariant field F]]

The tensorial time derivative <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> for a [[scalar field]] F defined on <math>\Sigma_{t}</math> is the [[derivative|rate of change]] in <math>F</math> in the instantaneously normal direction:

<math display="block">\frac{\delta F}{\delta t}=\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{F(P^*)-F(P)}{h}</math>

This definition is also illustrated in second geometric figure.

The above definitions are ''[[geometry|geometric]]''. In analytical settings, direct application of these definitions may not be possible. The CMS gives ''analytical'' definitions of C and <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> in terms of elementary operations from [[calculus]] and [[differential geometry]].

==Analytical definitions==

For [[mathematical analysis|analytical]] definitions of <math>C</math> and <math>\dot{\nabla}</math>, consider the evolution of <math>S</math> given by

<math display="block">Z^i = Z^i \left( t ,S \right) </math>

where <math>Z^{i}</math> are general [[curvilinear coordinates|curvilinear space coordinates]] and <math>S^{\alpha }</math> are the surface coordinates. By convention, tensor indices of function arguments are dropped. Thus the above equations contains <math>S</math> rather than <math>S^\alpha</math>. The velocity object <math>\textbf{V}=V^i\textbf{Z}_i</math> is defined as the [[partial derivative]]

<math display="block">V^i =\frac{\partial Z^i \left( t ,S \right)}{\partial t }</math>

The velocity <math>C</math> can be computed most directly by the formula

<math display="block">C=V^i N_i </math>

where <math>N_i</math> are the covariant components of the normal vector <math>\vec{N}</math>.

Also, defining the shift tensor representation of the surface's tangent space <math>Z^{\alpha}_{i}=\textbf{S}^\alpha\cdot\textbf{Z}_i</math> and the tangent velocity as <math>V^\alpha=Z^\alpha_iV^i</math> , then the definition of the <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> derivative for an [[Tensor field|invariant]] ''F'' reads

<math display="block">\dot{\nabla}F=\frac{\partial F\left( t ,S \right)}{\partial t }-V^\alpha\nabla _{\alpha }F</math>

where <math>\nabla_\alpha </math> is the covariant derivative on S.

For ''tensors'', an appropriate generalization is needed. The proper definition for a representative tensor <math>T^{i\alpha }_{j\beta }</math> reads

<math display="block">\dot{\nabla}T^{i\alpha }_{j\beta }=\frac{\partial T^{i\alpha }_{j\beta }}{\partial t}-V^{\eta }\nabla _{\eta }T^{i\alpha }_{j\beta }+V^{m}\Gamma ^{i}_{mk}T^{k\alpha }_{j\beta }-V^{m}\Gamma ^{k}_{mj}T^{i\alpha }_{k\beta }+\dot{\Gamma}^\alpha_\eta T^{i\eta }_{j\beta }-\dot{\Gamma}^\eta_\beta T^{i\alpha }_{j\eta }</math>

where <math>\Gamma^k_{mj}</math> are [[Christoffel symbols]] and <math>\dot{\Gamma}^\alpha_\beta=\nabla_\beta V^\alpha-C B^\alpha_\beta</math> is the surface's appropriate temporal symbols (<math>B^\alpha_\beta</math> is a matrix representation of the surface's curvature shape operator)

==Properties of the <math>\dot{\nabla}</math>-derivative==

The <math>\dot{\nabla}</math>-derivative commutes with contraction, satisfies the [[product rule]] for any collection of indices

<math display="block">\dot{\nabla}(S^i_\alpha T^\beta_j
 )=T^\beta_j\dot{\nabla}S^i_\alpha + S^i_\alpha\dot{\nabla}T^\beta_j</math>

and obeys a [[chain rule]] for surface [[Function (mathematics)#Restrictions and extensions|restrictions]] of spatial tensors:

<math display="block">\dot{\nabla}F^j_k(Z,t) =\frac{\partial F^j_k}{\partial t}+CN^i \nabla _i F^j_k</math>

Chain rule shows that the <math>\dot{\nabla}</math>-derivatives of spatial "metrics" vanishes

<math display="block">\dot{\nabla}\delta^i_j=0,\dot{\nabla}Z_{ij}=0,\dot{\nabla}Z^{ij}=0,\dot{\nabla}\varepsilon _{ijk}=0,\dot{\nabla}\varepsilon^{ijk}=0</math>

where <math>Z_{ij}</math> and <math>Z^{ij}</math> are covariant and contravariant [[metric tensor]]s, <math>\delta ^{i}_{j}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]] symbol,  and <math>\varepsilon _{ijk}</math> and <math>\varepsilon ^{ijk}</math> are the [[Levi-Civita symbol]]s. The [[Levi-Civita symbol|main article]] on Levi-Civita symbols describes them for [[Cartesian coordinate systems]]. The preceding rule is valid in general coordinates, where the definition of the Levi-Civita symbols must include the [[square root]] of the [[determinant]] of the covariant metric tensor <math>Z_{ij}</math>.

==Differentiation table for the <math>\dot{\nabla}</math>-derivative==

The <math>\dot{\nabla}</math> derivative of the key surface objects leads to highly concise and attractive formulas. When applied to the [[covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariant]] surface [[metric tensor]] <math>S_{\alpha \beta }</math> and the [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|contravariant]] metric tensor <math>S^{\alpha \beta }</math>, the following identities result

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{\nabla}S_{\alpha \beta } &=0 \\[8pt]
\dot{\nabla}S^{\alpha \beta } &=0
\end{align}</math>

where <math>B_{\alpha \beta }</math> and <math>B^{\alpha \beta }</math> are the doubly covariant and doubly contravariant [[Sectional curvature|curvature tensors]]. These curvature tensors, as well as for the mixed curvature tensor <math>B^\alpha_\beta</math>, satisfy

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{\nabla}B_{\alpha \beta }& = \nabla_\alpha \nabla_\beta C + CB_{\alpha \gamma }B^\gamma_\beta \\[8pt]
\dot{\nabla}B^\alpha_\beta& = \nabla_\beta\nabla^\alpha C + CB^\alpha_\gamma B^\gamma_\beta \\[8pt]
\dot{\nabla}B^{\alpha \beta }& = \nabla ^\alpha \nabla^\beta C + CB^{\gamma \alpha}B^\beta_\gamma
\end{align}</math>

The shift tensor <math>Z^i_\alpha</math> and the normal <math>N^i</math> satisfy

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{\nabla}Z^i_\alpha & = N^i\nabla _\alpha C \\[8pt]
\dot{\nabla}N^i & = -Z^i_\alpha \nabla^\alpha C
\end{align}</math>

Finally, the surface [[Levi-Civita symbol]]s <math>\varepsilon _{\alpha \beta }</math> and <math>\varepsilon ^{\alpha \beta }</math> satisfy

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\dot{\nabla} \varepsilon _{\alpha \beta } & = 0 \\[8pt]
\dot{\nabla} \varepsilon ^{\alpha \beta } & = 0
\end{align}</math>

== Time differentiation of integrals ==
The CMS provides rules for [[time evolution of integrals|time differentiation of volume and surface integrals]].
